It's the acid. The pan is fine.

Tomato sauce eats into the seasoning, especially on a long simmer. Where it wears thin, the bare iron underneath rusts, and that's the orange you're seeing. Oiling it warm is a good habit, but a coat of oil can't replace seasoning that's already gone. You have to bake new layers on:

1. Scrub the orange spots with steel wool and a little soap until they're gone.
2. Dry it on a burner for a few minutes.
3. Rub in a very thin coat of oil, then wipe off as much as you can so it looks almost dry.
4. Bake it upside down at about 450°F for an hour and let it cool in the oven.

Two or three rounds of that will bring it back. After that, quick tomato dishes are fine, but anything that simmers for more than half an hour should go in stainless or enameled, and don't leave sauce sitting in the cast iron after dinner.

A cast iron pan is only finished if it's cracked or warped badly enough to rock on the burner.

Plan on one to two hours a day. Before Day 1, open a free account on one email platform (MailerLite, Brevo and Mailchimp all have free plans) and use it for every hands-on task, so by the end you have a working setup of your own.

- Day 1: How email marketing works. The main types of email (newsletters, promotions, automated flows, transactional messages) and how a list turns into sales. Subscribe to a handful of brands you like and save their emails in a folder to study.
- Day 2: Permission and the law. Single and double opt-in, plus the basics of CAN-SPAM (US), GDPR (EU and UK) and CASL (Canada). Under CAN-SPAM, every marketing email needs a working unsubscribe link and a postal address.
- Day 3: Building a list. Signup forms, popups, landing pages and lead magnets like a discount code or a free checklist. Make a signup form and a landing page in your account.
- Day 4: Segmentation and personalization. Grouping subscribers by interest, purchase history, location or engagement, and using merge tags and dynamic content. Add yourself and a couple of friends as test subscribers, then set up tags and one segment.
- Day 5: Copywriting. Subject lines, preview text, body copy and calls to action. Write ten subject lines for the same email, then go through your saved folder and note which emails made you want to click.
- Day 6: Design. Templates, mobile layout, accessibility (alt text, contrast, readable font sizes) and when a plain-text look works better. Build a reusable template, using Canva for any graphics.
- Day 7: Your first campaign. Write a short newsletter, send a test to yourself on phone and desktop, fix what looks off, then send it to your test list.
- Day 8: Automation. Triggers, delays and conditions, and the standard flows: welcome series, abandoned cart, post-purchase and win-back.
- Day 9: A welcome series. Build three emails spread over about a week, triggered by your Day 3 form, and test it by signing up with a new address.
- Day 10: Deliverability. SPF, DKIM and DMARC, sender reputation, bounces, spam complaints and the bulk-sender requirements Gmail and Yahoo enforce. Look up a domain's records in MXToolbox and read through Google Postmaster Tools.
- Day 11: Metrics. Click rate, conversion rate, unsubscribes, bounces and spam complaints, and why open rates have been unreliable since Apple's Mail Privacy Protection. Learn to add UTM tags to links so email traffic shows up in Google Analytics.
- Day 12: A/B testing. What to test (subject lines, send times, calls to action), how big a sample you need, and how to avoid calling a winner too early. Set one up anyway; your test list is too small for meaningful results, but you'll learn how it works.
- Day 13: List hygiene. Bounce handling, re-engagement emails, and removing subscribers who haven't engaged in months, since inactive addresses drag down deliverability.
- Day 14: Strategy. How often to send, the mix of promotional and useful content, and planning a calendar. Map out a month of emails for a real or made-up business.
- Day 15: Capstone. Plan a full program for that business: lead magnet, signup form, welcome series, a monthly newsletter, one promotion, and the numbers you'd track. Then check it against what you learned on Days 10 and 11.

Other tools you'll run into: Klaviyo (common for online stores), HubSpot (email tied to a CRM), Litmus (previewing emails across inboxes) and Zapier (connecting forms and apps to your list).

Distance comes from several changes happening at once, all automated over the same two or three seconds. In any DAW with automation (Reaper, Logic, Ableton, Audition), put the voice on its own track and ramp these from the moment the fall starts:

1. Volume. Fade down 20 to 30 dB on a curve that starts slow and drops faster toward the end, since someone falling speeds up.
2. Low-pass filter. Sweep the cutoff from fully open down to around 1 to 2 kHz. High frequencies die off first over distance, so the voice gets duller as it drops.
3. Pitch. Bend it down one to three semitones over the fall. That's an exaggerated Doppler effect, and it's what makes the ear hear movement.
4. Reverb. Use a cave or stone-room preset and automate its mix from mostly dry to fully wet, so by the end you hear the space more than the voice. A short echo of around 150 ms with some feedback makes it sound like a deep shaft.
5. Stereo width. If the voice is in stereo, narrow it to mono as it falls so it shrinks to a point.

Let the reverb tail ring out after the voice ends, and add a faint thud at the end if the pit has a bottom.

In Audacity, use the Envelope tool for the fade and Sliding Stretch for the pitch drop. For the filter and reverb, split the clip into a few pieces and apply each effect a little stronger on each piece.

All numbers are per molecule of glucose.

| Stage | Where | Goes in | Comes out | ATP made |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Glycolysis | Cytoplasm | Glucose, 2 ATP, 2 NAD⁺ | 2 pyruvate, 4 ATP, 2 NADH | 2 net |
| Pyruvate oxidation | Mitochondrial matrix | 2 pyruvate, 2 NAD⁺ | 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂, 2 NADH | 0 |
| Krebs cycle | Mitochondrial matrix | 2 acetyl-CoA, 6 NAD⁺, 2 FAD | 4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP | 2 |
| Electron transport chain | Inner mitochondrial membrane | 10 NADH, 2 FADH₂, O₂ | Water, NAD⁺, FAD | About 26 to 28 |

**Glycolysis** splits one **glucose** (6 carbons) into two **pyruvate** (3 carbons each) in the **cytoplasm**. It doesn't need oxygen, so it's **anaerobic**. It spends 2 **ATP** to get started and makes 4, which is where the net 2 comes from. Those ATP are made by **substrate-level phosphorylation**, meaning an enzyme moves a phosphate group straight onto ADP. Electrons pulled off glucose go to the carrier **NAD⁺**, which becomes **NADH**.

Between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, each pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to **acetyl-CoA**, releasing one CO₂. This step is called **pyruvate oxidation** or the **link reaction**. Some classes count it as part of the Krebs cycle, so check how your teacher splits it.

The **Krebs cycle**, also called the **citric acid cycle**, runs in the **mitochondrial matrix**. Acetyl-CoA joins **oxaloacetate** to form **citrate**, and as the cycle goes around, the remaining carbons leave as **carbon dioxide** while electrons are loaded onto NADH and **FADH₂**. It turns twice per glucose, once for each acetyl-CoA.

The **electron transport chain** is a series of proteins in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**, whose folds are called **cristae**. NADH and FADH₂ hand their electrons to the chain, and the energy released as the electrons pass along is used to pump **hydrogen ions (H⁺)** into the **intermembrane space**. That builds a **proton gradient**. The H⁺ flow back through **ATP synthase**, which uses that flow to make ATP. The flow is called **chemiosmosis**, and making ATP this way is **oxidative phosphorylation**. **Oxygen** is the **final electron acceptor**: it picks up the used electrons and H⁺ and becomes **water**. Without oxygen, the chain backs up and stops.

Altogether that's about **30 to 32 ATP** per glucose. Older textbooks say **36 to 38** because they used higher estimates for the ATP made per NADH, so go with whatever number your class uses.

I'm going to start with the hard news, because you already know it and I don't want to dance around it.

We missed our third-quarter sales target by 18 percent. We closed the Dayton shop. And two of our managers have left the company.

That's a rough stretch, and I'm not going to stand up here and call it anything else. If you worked alongside the Dayton team or either of those managers, you've felt it more than most.

When a company has a quarter like that, people start bracing for cuts. I would too. So I want to tell you about two things that are not changing.

First, holiday hiring is still happening. We're bringing on extra help in the shops for the holidays, and we're not going to try to save money by skipping it. If you know someone who'd be good behind the counter at Roll & Rye this season, send them our way.

Second, the profit-share pool is not being cut. I'll say that one again, because I know it's been on a lot of minds. The profit-share pool is not being cut.

We made both of those decisions for the same reason. When sales drop, the quickest way to make the numbers look better is to pull back on the people doing the work. There are about 90 of us, and at that size, what each of you does shows up directly in how the company does. Cutting back on you would make the next quarter harder, so we're not doing it.

Getting that 18 percent back won't come from one big idea, and I'd be wary of anyone who says it will. It'll come from every shop doing the basics well for the rest of the year, starting with the customer in front of you. That means shelves that are full and fresh when the doors open, and an order that's right the first time. Customers notice that, and it's what brings them back.

It also means looking out for each other. Losing two managers has put more on some of your plates. If that's you, thank you. I know it hasn't been easy. And if something is getting in the way of good work, whether it's a schedule that doesn't hold up or equipment that keeps breaking, tell your manager or tell me. I'd like to hear about it now, while there's still time to fix it before the holidays.

I'm not going to pretend the next few months will be easy. The holidays are a lot of work in a bakery even in a good year, and this year we're doing it while we make up ground from a rough quarter. But you know how to do this work, and I've watched you do it well.

Home setups have made basic recording cheap, so a one-pager that leads with the room or the gear is selling the part that's easiest to replace. What associations still pay for is someone handling the hard parts for them. Their podcast is usually run by a comms or membership person on top of a full-time job, and the guests are members and executives who've never sat in front of a microphone.

That makes the engineer in the session your strongest point. Describe it by what the client gets: guests who've never been recorded still sound good on the first take, and problems get fixed during the session, so their staff isn't stuck reviewing fixes afterward. The live room is a supporting detail. It helps for panels and multi-guest episodes, but few clients choose a studio for its room.

The something else is the niche. A studio that only records for trade associations already knows the conference calendar, member spotlights, sponsor reads and the board or legal sign-off an episode has to clear before it goes out. A generalist studio or a home setup doesn't, so say it plainly and back it up with a few association names and a link to an episode.

For the page itself, I'd go in this order: who it's for, what a session with your engineer is like, what they get back and how fast, then client names and a starting price. Association staff usually need a number before they can take anything to budget approval.

# Why our AI policy stops at the numbers

By Rachel Nguyen, Operations Director

For the past six months, Ledger & Elm has worked under one rule for AI. Staff may use a writing assistant for first drafts of client emails. They may not use it on anything that touches numbers.

We're a 40-person accounting firm in Des Moines, and we wanted a rule short enough that nobody has to look it up. Anyone here can apply it without asking a manager, and any client can understand it in one read.

Client emails are a good fit for a writing assistant. Much of what accountants write to clients is routine, like deadline reminders and requests for missing documents, and some of it is hard to word well, like following up with a client who has stopped answering. A first draft gets the writer past the blank page, but the assistant doesn't know the client. The accountant who does still edits the draft, and it goes out under their name, so they're responsible for every word, the same as before.

Numbers are different work. Clients come to us to get them right, and a wrong figure can cost a client money in a way an awkward sentence can't. Writing assistants produce text that sounds sure of itself whether or not it's correct. In an email, a reviewer catches a clumsy phrase on the first read. In a return or a set of financial statements, a number that looks plausible and is wrong is one of the hardest mistakes to find.

"Anything that touches numbers" is broad. It covers the obvious work, like returns and financial statements, and smaller tasks too, like summarizing a spreadsheet or checking a total. A narrower rule with exceptions for simple calculations would mean someone deciding, in the middle of a busy season, whether a task is simple enough. We'd rather nobody has to make that call.

The rule means some work a tool could speed up still gets done by hand. For a firm whose job is getting numbers right, we're comfortable with that trade. Six months in, we're still working this way. If you're deciding where AI fits in your own firm, I'd start by asking what your clients pay you to get right. Keep the tools away from that work, and let them help with the writing around it.

1. Divide every term by 2, the number in front of x². Completing the square only works when x² has nothing in front of it. Divide all of the terms, including the -14 (and 0 ÷ 2 is still 0):

   x² + 6x - 7 = 0

2. Move the constant to the right side by adding 7 to both sides:

   x² + 6x = 7

3. Take half of the number in front of x and square it. Half of 6 is 3, and 3² = 9.

4. Add 9 to both sides (7 + 9 = 16):

   x² + 6x + 9 = 16

5. Factor the left side as a perfect square. It's always (x + the number you got by halving)², so here it's (x + 3)²:

   (x + 3)² = 16

6. Take the square root of both sides. Don't forget the ±, since both 4 and -4 square to 16:

   x + 3 = ±4

7. Split it into two equations:

   x + 3 = 4  or  x + 3 = -4

8. Subtract 3 from both sides of each:

   x = 1  or  x = -7

9. Check both answers in the original equation:
   - x = 1: 2(1)² + 12(1) - 14 = 2 + 12 - 14 = 0
   - x = -7: 2(-7)² + 12(-7) - 14 = 98 - 84 - 14 = 0

Both work, so x = 1 or x = -7.

With a number in front of x², the usual mistake is in step 1: dividing the x² and x terms by 2 but forgetting the -14. If your teacher wants you to factor the 2 out instead of dividing, you'd write 2(x² + 6x) = 14. When you add 9 inside the parentheses, you're adding 2 × 9 = 18 to the left side, so add 18 to the right side too: 2(x + 3)² = 32. Divide both sides by 2 and you're back at (x + 3)² = 16.

### Glycolysis

- Where: the **cytoplasm**. No **oxygen** needed.
- In: 1 **glucose**, 2 **ATP** (spent to get started), 2 **NAD⁺**
- Out: 2 **pyruvate**, 2 **NADH**
- ATP: 4 made by **substrate-level phosphorylation**, 2 spent, so a net gain of 2.

### Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle)

Between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, each **pyruvate** moves into the **mitochondrial matrix** and becomes **acetyl-CoA**, releasing one CO₂ and making one **NADH**.

- Where: the **mitochondrial matrix**
- In: **acetyl-CoA** (one per turn), plus **oxaloacetate**, which is regenerated each turn
- Out per turn: 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 **FADH₂**, 1 ATP (or GTP)
- Per glucose: two turns, so 4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, and 2 ATP

### Electron transport chain

- Where: the **inner mitochondrial membrane**, folded into **cristae**
- In: NADH and FADH₂ (electron donors), **O₂** (final electron acceptor), ADP and Pi
- Out: **H₂O**, plus NAD⁺ and FAD returned for reuse. Most of the ATP is made by **ATP synthase** as protons flow back across the membrane, a process called **chemiosmosis**.
- ATP: about 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂, so about 28 from 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂

### Totals

Per glucose, about 4 ATP come directly (2 from glycolysis, 2 from the Krebs cycle), and about 28 more come from the electron transport chain, for roughly 32. Textbooks differ. Newer ones give 30 to 32 and older ones 36 to 38, so check which number your class uses before Friday.

1. Volume: fade the voice down steadily so it sounds like it's getting farther from the mic.
2. Filter: sweep a low-pass filter down so the voice gets duller and more muffled, as if it's sinking into the pit.

Where We Let AI Write, and Where We Don't

Rachel Nguyen, Operations Director

At Ledger & Elm, a 40-person firm in Des Moines, we set a simple rule six months ago for how staff can use writing assistants. Anyone may use one to draft client emails. Nobody may use one on anything that touches numbers, whether that's a tax figure, a reconciliation, or a sentence describing an account balance.

We drew the line there for a reason. An email draft is low risk because a person reads it, edits it, and sends it under their own name. A number works differently. A writing assistant can produce a sentence that reads well and is wrong, and the error can be hard to spot in a paragraph. In our work, a wrong figure can matter a great deal, so numbers stay with people working from the source documents.

I think the same test works well beyond accounting. Before you decide where AI belongs in your work, ask what a wrong answer would cost you and whether anyone would catch it in time. A clumsy sentence in an email that a colleague reads before it goes out is a small problem. A wrong figure on a client's return is a different matter.

We also kept the rule simple on purpose. A rule that depends on judgment in the middle of a busy week tends to slip, especially near a deadline. A short list of what's allowed and what isn't holds up better.

Six months in, we're still using the same rule. Drafts can save time on wording, but the person sending the email still has to know the client and the file. That part was never going to be automated. Clients never see how a draft was written. They see whether their numbers are right, and that's the standard we hold ourselves to.

If you're setting this up at your firm, write your line down before someone needs it. A rule made under deadline pressure tends to be a worse one, so set yours while things are calm. Say what it covers, say who decides when a case doesn't fit, and review it once a year, since the tools will keep changing.

AI can help with a lot of the work around accounting. The question to answer first is where a mistake would be expensive and whether your process would catch it in time.

These counts are **per glucose molecule**, in a **eukaryotic cell**.

**Glycolysis** happens in the **cytoplasm**, specifically the **cytosol**. It splits **1 glucose** into **2 pyruvate**. It uses **2 ATP** upfront and makes **4 ATP**, giving **2 net ATP**. It also converts **2 NAD+** into **2 NADH**, which carry high-energy electrons. Water is another product. Glycolysis doesn't directly require oxygen.

Before the next stage, **pyruvate oxidation** happens in the **mitochondrial matrix**. The 2 pyruvate become **2 acetyl-CoA**, releasing **2 CO₂** and producing **2 NADH**. This step makes **no ATP**.

The **Krebs cycle**, also called the **citric acid cycle**, happens in the **mitochondrial matrix**. Its inputs include **2 acetyl-CoA**, **NAD+**, **FAD**, and ADP or GDP plus phosphate. It runs **twice per glucose**, producing **4 CO₂**, **6 NADH**, **2 FADH₂**, and energy equivalent to **2 ATP**. That energy is often first captured as **GTP**, which can transfer its phosphate to ADP to make ATP.

The **electron transport chain** is in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. **NADH** and **FADH₂** donate electrons. Their energy pumps **H+ ions** into the intermembrane space, building a gradient. **Oxygen** accepts the electrons at the end and combines with H+ to form **water**. **ATP synthase** uses the gradient to make ATP from **ADP and phosphate**. Together, electron transport and this ATP-making process are **oxidative phosphorylation**, producing about **26–28 ATP**. NAD+ and FAD are regenerated.

Altogether, that's about **30–32 ATP per glucose**: 2 from glycolysis, 2 from the Krebs cycle, and 26–28 from oxidative phosphorylation. The yield varies partly with how glycolysis's electrons are transferred into mitochondria.

3. Day 3: Learn consent and compliance. Cover permission, unsubscribe links, sender identification and applicable rules such as CAN-SPAM and GDPR. Write a signup statement. Don't buy lists or add people who haven't agreed to receive marketing.

4. Day 4: Learn your email platform. Explore contacts, tags, templates, campaigns and reports in Mailchimp or Brevo. Create a test audience using your own addresses or consenting testers.

5. Day 5: Study sender setup. Learn what SPF, DKIM and DMARC do, along with domain reputation. Review your platform's authentication instructions. Only change DNS settings for a domain you control.

6. Day 6: Build a signup form. Create a simple form or landing page in your platform. Give people a clear reason to subscribe, explain what they'll receive, and test the signup and confirmation process.

7. Day 7: Practice copywriting. Write an email with a subject line, preview text, useful body copy and one main call to action. Draft three subject lines in Google Docs, then choose one.

8. Day 8: Design for phones and accessibility. Build the email in your platform's editor. Check readable text, contrast, alt text and button size. Use Canva for an image if it adds useful information.

9. Day 9: Learn segmentation. Create sample segments for new subscribers and existing customers. Practice using tags and purchase or signup data. Make sure unsubscribe exclusions apply to every segment.

10. Day 10: Build an automation. Create a three-email welcome sequence. Learn triggers, delays, conditions and exit rules. Test that someone enters the sequence once and stops receiving marketing after unsubscribing.

11. Day 11: Plan campaigns and tracking. Make a simple email calendar in Sheets. Learn UTM tags with Google's Campaign URL Builder and how tracked visits appear in GA4 when it's configured. Check that the destination page matches the email's promise.

12. Day 12: Test delivery and rendering. Send to test inboxes, check mobile display, and test every link and the unsubscribe process. Learn bounce handling and suppression lists. Litmus or Email on Acid are optional tools for broader rendering tests.

13. Day 13: Learn reporting. Study delivery rate, unique clicks, conversions, unsubscribes and spam complaints. Practice calculating rates from sample data in Sheets. Apple Mail Privacy Protection can distort opens; security scanners can create automated clicks.

14. Day 14: Plan a split test. Change one thing, such as the subject line. Define the success metric and test duration before sending. A tiny practice list is useful for learning the setup, but won't establish a reliable winner.

15. Day 15: Run the practice campaign. Check the audience, authentication, copy, links and tracking. Send to your test addresses or a small permission-based list. Review the results and write down one change for the next campaign.

Make the voice quieter and duller as it recedes, with a dark echo that lasts after the direct voice disappears.

1. Put the voice on its own track and send it to a separate reverb track. That lets you fade the direct voice without cutting off the echo.

2. Automate the voice's volume downward. For a three-second fall, try ending about 24 dB below the starting level. Adjust the fade curve until the retreat sounds continuous.

3. Automate a low-pass filter to remove high frequencies as the voice gets farther away. Try moving the cutoff from around 10 kHz down to 2–3 kHz. Keep enough clarity to hear the voice at the start.

4. Use a dark reverb with a long tail. A decay of 3–5 seconds is a starting point. Let the reverb become more prominent relative to the direct voice, then fade it out too. A faint repeating delay can add echoes from the pit walls.

5. For a more dramatic fall, add a gradual downward pitch shift of about 1–3 semitones to suggest the Doppler effect. Keep it subtle unless you're making a cartoon effect. Pitch automation avoids slowing the words down.

For a pit directly below the microphone, keep the voice centered. Panning left or right would suggest sideways movement.

# Giving AI a defined job at work

By Rachel Nguyen, Operations Director, Ledger & Elm

The most useful workplace AI policy is one a person can apply while they're doing their job. A broad invitation to “use AI responsibly” leaves staff deciding what that means every time a task comes up.

At Ledger & Elm, our 40-person accounting firm in Des Moines, we've kept the rule specific. For six months, staff have been allowed to use a writing assistant for first drafts of client emails. They may not use it on anything that touches numbers.

That boundary follows the work we do. An assistant can propose language for a routine introduction or a request to arrange a conversation. An email discussing a balance, tax calculation or financial interpretation falls outside the rule, even when someone only wants help with the wording. Numbers can be affected by how a sentence describes them as well as by a calculation.

The first-draft limit also gives us a clear place for human judgment. Whoever sends an email needs to check that it says what they mean, reflects the facts and makes no commitment they aren't authorized to make. A polished sentence can still promise the wrong thing. The sender remains responsible for it.

Confidentiality needs its own check. Keeping numerical work out of the tool doesn't make every other piece of client information suitable for a prompt. A sensible policy should specify which tools are approved and what information staff may enter. People shouldn't have to guess whether a client name or a description of a sensitive situation is allowed.

For other firms considering AI, I'd start with a task that has a clear review point. Define what the assistant may produce, who checks it and what stays outside its scope. Use examples from ordinary work so staff can recognize the boundary without interpreting a policy from scratch.

Then evaluate the whole task. Drafting speed alone doesn't tell you whether a tool helps. Time spent correcting the draft belongs in that calculation, along with errors and the effort needed to check it. Staff should have a straightforward way to report drafts that create extra work.

A decision to expand the policy should name the new task and explain how errors would be caught before they reach a client. Approval for email drafting doesn't automatically extend to another task, however familiar the tool becomes.

Your pan is probably fine. On bare cast iron, orange patches usually mean rust. Tomato sauce can weaken the seasoning, especially during long simmers, leaving iron exposed to moisture. Three years of normal weeknight cooking wouldn't usually wear out the pan.

A warm wipe of oil doesn't remove rust. It can protect a dry surface, but repairing the seasoning needs a thin layer of oil cured with heat.

If your Hearth & Mill is uncoated, all-metal cast iron:

1. Scrub the rusty spots with warm water and dish soap. Steel wool is fine on bare iron where you're removing rust. Rinse.
2. Towel-dry, then heat it gently on the stove until all moisture is gone.
3. Wipe on a very thin layer of vegetable or canola oil, including the rusty areas. Wipe again with a clean cloth until it looks almost dry.
4. If the whole pan is oven-safe, bake it upside down at 450°F (230°C) for an hour, with ventilation, then let it cool in the oven.

For future tomato sauce, keep cooking time short and transfer leftovers out of the pan. Stainless steel or enameled cookware is easier for long acidic simmers.

If yours has an enamel coating, skip steel wool and reseasoning. Orange could be staining or exposed metal at a chip. Stop using it if the cooking surface has flaking enamel or the pan is cracked.

   \[
   (x + 3)^2 = 16
   \]

10. Take the square root of both sides. Remember the plus or minus:

   \]

   \[
   x + 3 = 4
   \]

   x = 1
   \]

   \]

   \[

   \]

Cast iron can handle acidic food for a short time, but tomato sauce is rough on seasoning, especially if it simmers for a while or sits in the pan after cooking. Once the seasoning thins, water and acid can reach the iron. Oil helps, but it won't fix bare spots by itself.

Do this:

1. Scrub the orange spots off with a stiff brush or chainmail scrubber.
2. Dry the pan on heat until it's fully dry.
3. Rub on a very thin coat of oil, then heat it until it just starts to smoke.
4. Repeat once or twice if the surface still looks patchy.
5. Avoid long tomato cooks for a bit while the seasoning builds back up.

A three-year-old Hearth & Mill pan with normal use should be fine. It's asking for a little reseasoning, not retirement.

**Glycolysis** happens in the **cytoplasm**.

It breaks down **glucose** into two smaller molecules called **pyruvate**.

What goes in:

- **1 glucose**
- **2 ATP** to start the process
- **2 NAD+**
- **ADP** and phosphate

What comes out:

- **2 pyruvate**
- **4 ATP made**, but **2 net ATP** because 2 were used at the start
- **2 NADH**

So the ATP total for glycolysis is **2 net ATP**.

**Krebs cycle**, also called the **citric acid cycle**, happens in the **mitochondrial matrix**.

Before it starts, **pyruvate** is changed into **acetyl-CoA**, which releases **carbon dioxide** and makes **NADH**.

What goes in for one glucose total:

- **2 acetyl-CoA**
- **NAD+**
- **FAD**
- **ADP** and phosphate

What comes out for one glucose total:

- **4 carbon dioxide**
- **6 NADH**
- **2 FADH2**
- **2 ATP**

So the ATP total for the Krebs cycle is **2 ATP**.

The **electron transport chain** happens in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**.

This is where most of the ATP is made. **NADH** and **FADH2** drop off high-energy electrons. The electrons move through proteins in the membrane, and that energy pumps **hydrogen ions** across the membrane. When hydrogen ions flow back through **ATP synthase**, ATP is made.

What goes in:

- **NADH**
- **FADH2**
- **oxygen**
- **ADP** and phosphate

What comes out:

- **ATP**
- **water**
- **NAD+**
- **FAD**

The ATP total for the electron transport chain is about **26 to 28 ATP**.

For one glucose molecule, cellular respiration usually makes about **30 to 32 ATP total**:

- **Glycolysis: 2 ATP**
- **Krebs cycle: 2 ATP**
- **Electron transport chain: 26 to 28 ATP**

Six Months of Using AI Carefully at Ledger & Elm

By Rachel Nguyen, Operations Director, Ledger & Elm

Six months ago, we made a small change at Ledger & Elm: our staff could use a writing assistant for first drafts of client emails.

We also made a firm rule at the same time. They could not use it on anything that touches numbers.

That rule has served us well.

We’re a 40-person accounting firm in Des Moines, and our work depends on accuracy, judgment, and trust. A clear email helps a client understand what we need from them. A wrong number can create a much bigger problem. So we decided to separate the two.

AI can be useful for getting past a blank page. It can help draft a polite reminder, simplify a long explanation, or turn rough notes into a more organized message. For staff who write a lot of client emails every week, that can save time and make the work feel less repetitive.

But we don’t ask it to calculate, interpret, verify, or summarize financial details. If a message includes figures, tax information, payroll details, deadlines tied to filings, or anything from a client’s books, the work stays with our people and our normal review process.

That boundary has made adoption easier. Staff don’t have to guess where the line is. If it’s language, a writing assistant may help with a first draft. If it touches numbers, it doesn’t go in.

We’ve also learned that a first draft is only a first draft. The person sending the message is still responsible for tone, accuracy, context, and final approval. Our clients are not writing to software. They’re writing to us.

After six months, the biggest benefit hasn’t been speed alone. It’s been confidence. A staff member can start with a rough version and then make it sound like themselves. A manager can spend less time helping someone phrase a routine message and more time on the client issue behind it.

AI at work does not need to start with a sweeping transformation. For us, it started with one narrow use case and one clear limit.

That’s the approach I’d recommend to other small firms. Pick a low-risk workflow. Define what the tool can do. Define what it cannot do. Keep people accountable for the final work.

Used carefully, AI can help a team communicate better without changing the standards clients count on.

You want the voice to get farther away, lower in detail, and more surrounded by space as it “falls.” You can do that with a few effects changing over time.

Start with volume automation. Make the voice fade down steadily, faster at first if the fall is sudden, then slower as it gets distant.

Add reverb and increase it as the voice falls. Use a large cave, tunnel, or chamber reverb. As the voice gets farther away, raise the wet reverb level and lower the dry voice level.

Use EQ to remove clarity over time. Roll off high frequencies so the voice gets muffled. You can also cut some low end if you want it to feel farther away, or boost low echo if you want a big pit sound.

Add delay or echo. A short slap at the start can become longer, darker echoes as the person falls deeper. Keep the repeats quieter than the voice.

Add panning if you want movement. If the person falls past the mic, pan the voice quickly from center to one side, then let the echo spread wider in stereo.

A simple effect chain would be:

1. Volume automation fading down
2. EQ, with highs rolling off over time
3. Reverb, increasing over time
4. Delay, increasing slightly as the voice gets distant
5. Optional pitch drop if you want a stylized fall

If you’re doing it in Audacity, GarageBand, Logic, Premiere, Resolve, or Audition, look for volume automation, reverb, EQ, delay, and panning. The main trick is automation, not just adding one effect once.

1. Volume automation: gradually reduce level (gain) over the pass, starting subtle and ending −12 to −18 dB.
2. EQ sweep: automate a low‑pass filter so highs roll off as the voice moves away (start clear, move cutoff down to ~2–3 kHz or lower).
3. Reverb send: increase reverb wet/dry and choose a long, dark reverb (large hall or convolution). Increase early reflections and decay slightly as it falls.
4. Delay: add a subtle slapback or slow delay with high damping, increasing wet as the voice recedes for echoes.
5. Stereo and distance: automate a small increase in stereo width and add subtle high‑frequency damping; optionally apply a downward pitch shift (a few cents) to imply Doppler, but keep it subtle.

Do this in any DAW: put the EQ and gain on the track and automate, use a send to a reverb and increase send level, and add a timed delay. Test with headphones and tweak the EQ cutoff and reverb decay until it feels like it’s dropping away.

Solve 2x² + 12x - 14 = 0 by completing the square — numbered steps:

1. Divide every term by the coefficient of x² (2) to make the x² coefficient 1:
   x² + 6x - 7 = 0

   x² + 6x = 7

Six months ago, Ledger & Elm put our first formal rule about artificial intelligence on the books. We are a 40-person accounting firm in Des Moines, so our clients rely on us for accuracy, discretion, and reliable financial records. When generative software became widely available, we decided against an outright ban. Instead, we established one clear boundary.

Our staff may use an AI writing assistant to draft ordinary client emails. They may never use it on anything that touches numbers.

That means tax returns, audit schedules, reconciliations, and payroll reviews remain strictly human work. Staff do not paste client figures into a prompt window, and we do not use software to summarize financial data. Language models predict text, and calculation requires accounting software and human oversight. In accounting, an answer that sounds right but misses by two thousand dollars is useless.

Where the software helps is with routine office correspondence. Many accountants understand complex tax regulations but spend fifteen minutes figuring out how to ask a client for a missing form. Letting software generate a rough draft helps staff get started. Every email is still reviewed, edited, and sent by the person whose name is on the signature, but starting from a draft saves hours each week across the firm.

Six months in, this rule works because staff members do not have to interpret a complicated handbook. If a task involves numbers or client files, the tool stays closed. If someone is writing a routine update or scheduling a review, they can use a draft assistant to clear their inbox faster.

We expect the technology to change, and we will update our guidelines as new tools appear. For now, keeping draft software away from financial figures protects our client relationships and gives our team room to work efficiently.

1. **Glycolysis**
Location: The **cytoplasm**.
Inputs: One molecule of **glucose**, two molecules of **NAD+**, and two molecules of **ADP**.
Outputs: Two molecules of **pyruvate**, two molecules of **NADH**, and four molecules of **ATP**.
ATP yield: 2 net **ATP** (two are consumed in the preparatory phase, four are produced).

2. The **Krebs cycle** (also called the **citric acid cycle**)
Location: The **mitochondrial matrix**.
Inputs: Two molecules of **acetyl-CoA** (produced from pyruvate during the link reaction), six molecules of **NAD+**, two molecules of **FAD**, and two molecules of **ADP**.
Outputs: Four molecules of carbon dioxide, six molecules of **NADH**, two molecules of **FADH2**, and two molecules of **ATP**.
ATP yield: 2 **ATP** per glucose molecule (one per cycle turn).

3. The **electron transport chain** and **chemiosmosis**
Location: The **inner mitochondrial membrane**.
Inputs: Electrons delivered by **NADH** and **FADH2**, molecular **oxygen**, and **ADP**.
Outputs: **Water**, regenerated **NAD+**, regenerated **FAD**, and **ATP**.
ATP yield: Approximately 26 to 28 **ATP** produced as protons flow through **ATP synthase**.

Total yield: Roughly 30 to 32 **ATP** per glucose molecule across all three stages.

Tomato sauce is acidic enough to dissolve polymerized seasoning down to bare metal. Once bare iron is exposed to moisture and air, it forms surface rust immediately, which is the orange layer you see. Wiping oil on a warm pan will not protect it if the underlying seasoning layer is gone.

4. Place the pan upside down in your oven at 450°F for one hour, then turn off the oven and let it cool completely inside.

Cook with fats and non-acidic foods for a few weeks to strengthen the seasoning before using tomatoes in it again.

The pan isn't finished. Tomato sauce is acidic enough to strip seasoning, and bare cast iron rusts orange once that layer is gone. Oiling it warm after you cook does not rebuild the seasoning. It only wets the metal.

Dry it on a burner until no moisture is left, wipe on a thin coat of whatever cooking oil you already use, and heat it until the oil stops smoking. Once or twice is enough to start. It will look blotchy. Ordinary weeknight cooking will darken it again.

**Glycolysis** happens in the **cytoplasm**. It does not use oxygen.

In: one **glucose**, and 2 **ATP** spent to start the pathway. Out: 2 **pyruvate**, 2 **NADH**, and 4 ATP made. Net is **2 ATP** per glucose. Most of the energy is still in the pyruvate. This step only splits the sugar.

Each pyruvate then moves into the mitochondrion and becomes **acetyl-CoA**. That happens in the **mitochondrial matrix**. Per glucose you get 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 **CO2**, and 2 NADH. No ATP there.

The **Krebs cycle** (also called the **citric acid cycle**) also runs in the mitochondrial matrix. One turn per acetyl-CoA, so two turns per glucose. In: 2 acetyl-CoA. Out: 4 CO2, 6 NADH, 2 **FADH2**, and **2 ATP**. The cycle does not use oxygen itself. It stalls if the chain stalls, because the chain regenerates **NAD+** and **FAD**.

The **electron transport chain** is on the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. In: electrons from NADH and FADH2, plus **oxygen**. Out: **water**. Oxygen is the **final electron acceptor**. The chain pumps protons, and **ATP synthase** lets them flow back to make ATP. This is where most of the ATP comes from. Classes still often say about **34 ATP** from the chain and **36 to 38** total per glucose. Newer counts are closer to **28 to 34** from the chain and about **30 to 32** total, because each NADH is not a flat 3 ATP. Use your teacher's number on Friday. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle make a little ATP directly, and the chain makes most of it.

Locations, for the card: cytoplasm, mitochondrial matrix, inner mitochondrial membrane.

Six months ago, Ledger & Elm set one rule for AI at work. Staff may use a writing assistant for first drafts of client emails. They may not use it on anything that touches numbers. We are a 40-person accounting firm in Des Moines. I run operations, so I find out quickly whether people can follow that rule on a Tuesday in March.

The two kinds of work fail in different ways. A stiff email is a nuisance. The sender can fix it before it goes out, and the client can ask if something is unclear. A wrong number is a different kind of mistake. It can travel inside a return, a schedule, or a note to a client, and the sentences around it will sound calm either way. A writing model does not flag its own arithmetic. We do not ask it to try. If a document has a figure or a calculation in it, the assistant stays closed.

The email permission is narrow. A lot of our client mail is scheduling, a request for documents, or a plain recap of a decision a person already made. None of that requires the tool to see a balance. The draft is a starting point for the opening lines, which is where people lose time. The staff member who owns the relationship still reads every sentence, still sends the email, and still owns whatever comes back. If the draft invents a deadline, or sounds warmer than we are with that client, the sender cuts it. We did not hand that judgment to the software.

Staff use the assistant the firm approved. They do not paste client files into a public site because a sentence was hard. Client information stays in our systems.

After six months, I have not added a second rule. A longer policy would look more official and get followed less, especially once filing season starts and nobody has time to reread it. New staff hear the same sentence in week one. First drafts of client emails are allowed. Anything that touches numbers is not. Managers can repeat it without opening a document.

If you run a firm like this one, write the permission and the ban in that same sentence. Do not announce a program you have not defined, and do not ask people to use the tool so you can say they did. Leave the rule in place long enough to see if it survives a busy season. Ours is still the line we started with, six months on.

The number in front of x^2 is 2, so get that down to 1 before you complete the square. If you add the completing number while the 2 is still there, the right side is wrong.

1. Write the equation.
2x^2 + 12x - 14 = 0

2. Add 14 to both sides so the constant moves to the right.
2x^2 + 12x - 14 + 14 = 0 + 14
2x^2 + 12x = 14

3. Divide both sides by 2, the coefficient of x^2. Divide every term, including the right side.
2x^2 / 2 + 12x / 2 = 14 / 2
x^2 + 6x = 7

4. The coefficient of x is now 6. Take half of it.
6 / 2 = 3

5. Square that result. This is the number that completes the square.
3^2 = 9

6. Add 9 to both sides of the equation from step 3.
x^2 + 6x + 9 = 7 + 9
x^2 + 6x + 9 = 16

7. Factor the left side. Half of 6 was 3, and 6x is positive, so the factor is (x + 3).
(x + 3)^2 = 16

8. Take the square root of both sides. Keep both the positive root and the negative root.
x + 3 = 4 or x + 3 = -4

9. Subtract 3 from both sides of the first equation.
x + 3 - 3 = 4 - 3
x = 1

10. Subtract 3 from both sides of the second equation.
x + 3 - 3 = -4 - 3
x = -7

11. Check x = 1 in the original equation.
2(1)^2 + 12(1) - 14 = 2 + 12 - 14 = 0

12. Check x = -7 in the original equation.
2(-7)^2 + 12(-7) - 14 = 2(49) - 84 - 14 = 98 - 84 - 14 = 0

Both check. The solutions are x = 1 and x = -7.

If you had added 9 before dividing by 2, you would have needed to add 2 times 9, which is 18, on the right side. Dividing first is what keeps that from happening.

AI at Work, on Our Terms

By Rachel Nguyen, Ops Director, Ledger & Elm

When people talk about AI in professional services, the story often jumps straight to full automation. At Ledger & Elm, a 40-person accounting firm in Des Moines, we took a narrower path. For the past six months we have used a writing assistant in one place only: first drafts of client emails. Everything that touches numbers stays human.

That line is not a slogan. It is how we protect the work clients hire us for.

Email is full of blank-page time. A clear opener, a polite chase on a missing document, a plain-language note after a call: a writing assistant can get a draft on the screen faster so staff spend their attention on tone, facts, and whether the message is ready to send. Someone still writes the final version. Someone still hits send. The tool drafts; the person decides.

Numbers are different. Journal entries, reconciliations, tax figures, workpapers, anything that feeds a return or a report: we do not run those through a writing assistant. Accounting mistakes do not announce themselves in polished prose. They show up as wrong totals, missed adjustments, and confidence that should not have been there. Our rule is simple. If the task is about getting language started, the assistant is allowed. If the task is about getting a figure right, it is not.

Six months in, the split has held. People use the tool where it saves time and leave it alone where it would create risk. New staff learn the boundary in onboarding the same way they learn our review process. Clients do not need a lecture on our software stack. They need to know a person here is accountable for their numbers.

We are not anti-technology. We are pro-judgment. AI can help with the blank page. It does not replace the professional who signs off on the work.

If other small firms are sorting out the same question, start with a written boundary, keep it short, and enforce it the same way every week. Ours is one sentence: drafts for client email, never for numbers. That has been enough to get value without blurring the part of the job we cannot hand off.

**Glycolysis** happens in the **cytoplasm**. **Glucose** (6-carbon) goes in and is split into two **pyruvate** (3-carbon) molecules. You also get a net of **2 ATP** and **2 NADH**. No oxygen required.

The **Krebs cycle** (also called the **citric acid cycle**) happens in the **mitochondrial matrix**. Each **pyruvate** is first converted to **acetyl-CoA**, which enters the cycle. Per glucose (two turns), outputs are **2 ATP** (technically GTP in some texts, counted as ATP), **6 NADH**, **2 FADH₂**, and **CO₂** as waste. Still no O₂ used directly here.

The **electron transport chain** is on the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. **NADH** and **FADH₂** drop off electrons; those move through the chain and help pump protons, building a gradient. **Oxygen** is the final electron acceptor and becomes **water**. ATP synthase uses the gradient to make most of the ATP: about **~28–34 ATP** from oxidative phosphorylation, depending on the textbook’s counting. Combined with glycolysis and Krebs, complete aerobic respiration is often summarized as about **~30–38 ATP** per glucose.

Flashcard anchors: **where** (cytoplasm vs matrix vs inner membrane), **in** (glucose / acetyl-CoA / NADH·FADH₂·O₂), **out** (pyruvate·NADH·ATP / CO₂·NADH·FADH₂·ATP / H₂O·lots of ATP).

Solve \(2x^2 + 12x - 14 = 0\) by completing the square.

1. Write the equation: \(2x^2 + 12x - 14 = 0\).

2. Move the constant to the right side: \(2x^2 + 12x = 14\).

3. Divide every term by 2 (the coefficient on \(x^2\)) so the \(x^2\) term is alone:
   \(x^2 + 6x = 7\).

4. Take half of the \(x\) coefficient: half of 6 is 3. Square it: \(3^2 = 9\).

5. Add 9 to both sides:
   \(x^2 + 6x + 9 = 7 + 9\).

6. The left side is a perfect square:
   \((x + 3)^2 = 16\).

7. Square root both sides (remember ±):
   \(x + 3 = \pm 4\).

8. Split into two equations:
   \(x + 3 = 4\) or \(x + 3 = -4\).

9. Solve:
   \(x = 1\) or \(x = -7\).

10. Check in the original if you want credit insurance: both work.

Answer: \(x = 1\) or \(x = -7\).

This is usually a seasoning issue, not “the pan is bad,” but the acid is part of it.

Tomato sauce is acidic enough to loosen a thin or uneven seasoning layer. If the pan had any bare or patchy spots, the acid can expose the iron underneath, and then the iron oxidizes and shows that orange/rusty look. That doesn’t necessarily mean the pan is ruined; it just means the seasoning is no longer protecting the metal evenly.

Three years of normal use is not a short lifespan for cast iron, and a Hearth & Mill pan should be fine. The most likely explanation is: the pan is not fully seasoned in those spots, or the seasoning is getting stripped in a few areas by repeated acid exposure plus heat.

What to do:

- scrub the orange areas gently
- rinse and dry thoroughly
- re-season the pan with a thin coat of oil and bake/heat it until it polymerizes
- avoid leaving tomato sauce in it for long after cooking
- use a little more frequent maintenance if the pan is not staying evenly dark

If it’s just a patchy orange tint and not flaky rust, I’d call it a seasoning problem with acid as the trigger, not a finish defect.

The classic move is to make the voice start close, then pull it away in space and volume while the room tone and reverb grow behind it.

Simple recipe:

- start with a dry, close-mic recording
- automate the voice to get quieter and farther from the mic over a few seconds
- add a longer, darker reverb tail as it moves away
- roll off some high end and maybe reduce the top a bit so it feels more distant
- add a little low-frequency rumble or a subtle pitch drop to make it feel like it’s falling away
- if you want “pit” energy, bring in a resonant swoop or reverse tail under it, then fade the source back into the room

The key is the change over time, not just one effect. A single reverb won’t sell it. You need the voice to literally feel like it is receding: smaller, softer, thinner, and farther away from the listener.

If you want a more dramatic version, start with a close, intimate vocal, then send it through a long, dark tail with a low-pass filter and automate a gradual distance curve. That gives the impression of falling into a cavern or pit.

TL;DR: the worker release was deployed with a missing queue-prefix configuration, so workers started polling the wrong queue and never delivered customer events. No customer data was lost, no requests need to be resent, and delivery was restored after rollback.

What broke: the production deployment expected a queue-prefix environment variable that wasn’t present. Because of that, workers started polling an empty queue instead of the active customer queue. They stayed running and reported healthy process status, which made the release look successful even though nothing was being delivered.

What we lost: nothing. No events were lost, and the application interface and inbound API stayed up. Customers do not need to resend their requests. The backlog was replayed after rollback and normal delivery resumed before the replay finished.

Why we missed it: staging had the variable in a developer-managed config file, and the release checklist checked worker startup but not whether production workers were actually pointing at the right queue. The alerting was watching failed delivery attempts, but no attempts were being made, so the issue never triggered.

Next fix: the worker must refuse to start if the queue prefix is missing instead of falling back silently. There also needs to be a queue-age alert that catches waiting events even when there are no failed attempts.

For a neighborhood tool library, the best north star is not “more members.” It’s “more members who actually use the library, return items, and keep the shared system healthy.”

Right now, having 220 members and only about 40 active borrowers means the real question is not whether we’re attracting people, but whether we’re converting interest into consistent participation. A member who signs up once and never borrows is not the same as a member who is engaged, returns gear on time, and tells other people about the library.

I’d suggest a north star like this: “Build a thriving, trusted local borrowing network where members actively participate, share tools, and keep the library circulating.”

From there, track the measures that matter: active members, repeat borrowers, return rate, tool utilization, volunteer hours, and member referrals. If we grow member count without increasing use, we’re just adding inventory to a waiting list. If we grow active use and strong return habits, we’re building a real community resource.

Here’s the full process for solving 2x^2 + 12x - 14 = 0 by completing the square.

1. Divide every term by 2 so the coefficient of x^2 is 1.
   2x^2 + 12x - 14 = 0
   x^2 + 6x - 7 = 0

2. Move the constant to the other side.
   x^2 + 6x = 7

3. Take half of the x coefficient, then square it.
   The coefficient of x is 6.
   Half of 6 is 3.
   3^2 = 9

4. Add 9 to both sides.
   x^2 + 6x + 9 = 7 + 9
   x^2 + 6x + 9 = 16

5. Factor the left side.
   (x + 3)^2 = 16

6. Take the square root of both sides.
   x + 3 = ±4

7. Solve for x.
   x + 3 = 4  gives  x = 1
   x + 3 = -4 gives  x = -7

Final answer: x = 1 or x = -7

This proposal is a low-risk way to test whether reusable delivery totes are practical for our kitchen customer base. The issue is simple: disposable packaging creates waste and paper bags fail when chilled items condense, while a full fleet replacement would be expensive and premature without proof that customers will return containers and that depot washing can handle the load.

The proposal would run an eight-week trial from 2 November to 27 December at the Elm Quay and Ridge Row depots. It would use 600 totes, offered voluntarily to selected business customers with regular deliveries. The trial keeps disposable packaging available as a backup, and it avoids any new app or integration by using numbered tote labels tied to each delivery.

The requested budget is $18,600, covering containers, washing, labels, and staff training. The main operational success gate is at least 85% of totes returned within 10 calendar days. We would also track driver feedback and damaged containers so we don’t mistake a good return rate for a process that is still impractical.

The key point for decision-making is that this is a trial, not an approval for rollout. Lena Voss would own the operational trial, and Hari Mendel would present an expansion recommendation on 8 January 2027 if the pilot performs well. If returns are poor, we should fix the process before we expand or blame customers for a system they were never asked to perfect.

You don’t need a full contract to test the idea, but you do need a real plan: a target market, a pricing model, a rough cash runway, a way to handle insurance and licenses, and a reason to believe you can turn those soft commitments into actual jobs.

If I were in your shoes, I’d stay until there’s a signed contract or at least a clear backlog with real work lined up. Not forever, but long enough to not leave on hope. Starting a residential company can be a good move, but it’s a business move, not a leap of faith. Treat it like that.

If those builders do turn into work and you can see the numbers make sense, then it may be the right time. But I wouldn’t call it “the move” just because they said they’ll call. That’s not a plan yet.

I’d rather you leave with a contract in hand than with a story and a wish.
